old:
Leverage, currency mismatch and the 2029-2030 refinancing. Net debt is S/3,252M, 3.6x the S/897M Adjusted LTM EBITDA, and LTM EBIT covered interest expense only 0.95x (FiscalAI). Cash interest and hedge premiums were S/201M in 1H26 alone. Part of the debt is in USD and MXN while Peru and Colombia earn in PEN and COP: in 1H26 a 4% PEN depreciation against the MXN and 1% against the USD added S/117M of gross debt with no new borrowing. S/761M of loans falls due between July 2029 and June 2030 and S/1,284M after that, including the term loan maturing in 2030 that the Omaha case assumes is refinanced.

Equity is only about a quarter of EV, so if Mexico and Colombia EBITDA does not grow, Auna refinances at 3.5x or more at whatever spread the market asks then, and each 0.5x of EV/EBITDA multiple is worth roughly $1.70-2.30 per share. A price near $4 would also test the unofficial loan-to-value level on Enfoca's pledged Class B shares.
new: Net debt S/3,252M is 3.6x Adjusted LTM EBITDA; LTM EBIT covered interest only 0.95x. FX mismatch added S/117M of debt in 1H26. S/761M falls due July 2029-June 2030; without EBITDA growth, refinancing hurts thin equity.

old: The equity has almost no cushion. Net debt of £1,545M is 8.9x LTM adjusted EBITDA (£174M), and capex of about £300-350M a year plus about £160-190M of cash interest exceeds any EBITDA the company has ever reported (record: £306M in FY2023). Cumulative burn over FY2027-FY2029 is about £700M in the base case, against pro forma liquidity of about £340M. The March 2029 notes ($1,050M + £565M) must be refinanced, and the USD notes were reported at about 57 cents (yield to maturity about 37%) after the HPS deal. If the refinancing comes with an exchange into shares, existing equity is worth close to zero (the bear case).
new: Almost no equity cushion: net debt £1,545M is 8.9x LTM adjusted EBITDA; capex plus interest exceed record EBITDA. Burn of about £700M exceeds £340M liquidity; a March 2029 debt-for-shares exchange leaves equity near zero.

old: Governance and creditor conflict. The four strategic blocs hold 68.5% (Yew Tree/Stroll 32.99%, Geely 14.08%, PIF 13.88%, Mercedes-Benz 7.54%), and several deals were done with the controlling shareholder: the F1 naming rights sold to AMR GP for £50M, the sale of the AMR GP stake, and the £50M Yew Tree facility. The July 2026 financing moved almost 200 trademarks into an unrestricted subsidiary and committed 50.1% of the non-automotive brand rights to Authentic Brands. Bondholders threaten to challenge it. If a court unwinds the deal, liquidity falls back toward £145M (H1 2026 before the financing). If it stands, the most durable asset is partly outside the group.
new: Governance and creditor conflict: four blocs hold 68.5%, with related-party deals. The July 2026 financing moved almost 200 trademarks into an unrestricted subsidiary; bondholders threaten to challenge. Unwound, liquidity falls toward £145M.

old: Demand and the Valhalla cliff. The FY2026 figures depend on about 500 Valhallas (225 delivered in H1 2026), a limited series whose orders currently run to the end of Q4 2026. No successor Specials programme has been announced. Core demand is weak. Core wholesales fell from 5,812 (FY2024) to 5,266 (FY2025), APAC fell 21% in FY2025 as China's luxury tax changed, and the US quota admits only 100,000 UK cars a year at 10% (27.5% above that; 25,000 per quarter from 2026). Core ASP fell 5% in H1 2026 on dealer support. Without Valhalla, LTM revenue would be about £200-250M lower (hypothesis based on the implied Specials ASP).
new: Valhalla cliff: FY2026 depends on about 500 Valhallas, with no successor Specials announced. Core is weak: wholesales fell from 5,812 (FY2024) to 5,266 (FY2025). Without Valhalla, LTM revenue would be about £200-250M lower (hypothesis).

old:
Oncosalud is the core of the moat: plan memberships reached 1,472 thousand in 2Q26 (+6% YoY, +2% QoQ), helped by about 7,000 SEDAPAL members from a new B2B policy, while oncological plans were 1,005 thousand (+1%). A distressed exchange transfers the equity to creditors. The HPS term loan matures July 2031 (whether it has a springing maturity linked to the 2029 notes is not verified).

old: Auna is a Peruvian a vertical integrated healthcare (insurer and provider) company with significant potential to capture TAM in Mexico and Colombia, as the success of its business model has already been demonstrated in Peru. Auna is a network of clinical services that includes oncology services (Oncosalud), consultations, surgeries, and healthcare membership plans. It operates around 31 total facilities, 2.3k beds and 1.5M healthcare plans. Around Peru, it has 6 main clinics, in Colombia, it has around 8 centers (1.1k beds), and in Mexico, 3. The rest are medical centers around these countries. This network enables patients to receive medical care in different parts of Peru and LATAM.
new: Auna is a Peruvian vertically integrated healthcare company (insurer and provider) with significant TAM to capture in Mexico and Colombia, its model already proven in Peru. Its network spans Oncosalud oncology, consultations, surgeries and plans: around 31 facilities, 2.3k beds and 1.5M healthcare plans.

old: Because its business model differs from traditional private hospitals (vertical integrated model, Oncosalud sells plans and Auna attends patients), Auna's network makes it unique. Its closest competitors are Brazilian and Mexican, and if we value the company using comparable multiples, there is significant upside potential for Auna. For any refutating this, the valuation for FCF is also solid (even excluding 2Q26 that was a one time supplier financing)
new: Its vertically integrated model (Oncosalud sells plans, Auna treats patients) makes Auna's network unique versus traditional private hospitals. Against Brazilian and Mexican comparables there is significant upside, and the FCF valuation is also solid, even excluding the one-time 2Q26 supplier financing.

old:
There are two main catalysts for Auna:

Torre Treca: This is a Peruvian government facility that has been ceded to Auna following a contract that was disputed for several years. This represents potential revenue with zero or minimal CapEx required for remodeling.

Recovery of operations in Mexico and Colombia: Disagreements with suppliers (doctors), lose of volume, mix of contracts, talent overhaul, payers, and government clients caused the company to lose money during the first years they were established there. Now, with more experience in these geographies, they are showing signs of recovery. Once these markets mature, EBITDA and profit could increase significantly.
new: Two catalysts: Torre Treca, a Peruvian government facility ceded to Auna after years of dispute, adds revenue with minimal remodeling CapEx; and recovery in Mexico and Colombia, where supplier, volume, contract and payer problems caused early losses. Maturing, EBITDA and profit could rise significantly.

old: LEN trades at a discount during the down-cycle, with margins compressed by buyer incentives and mortgage-rate buydowns and ASP declining — pressures that are cyclical and consistent with peak pessimism. A structural undersupply of housing in the US underpins long-term demand. As the #2 homebuilder by scale, LEN would capture a disproportionate share of the volume-×-margin rebound once mortgage rates ease. The thesis buys the normalized earnings power, not the depressed current level.
new: LEN trades at a down-cycle discount, with margins compressed by incentives and rate buydowns and ASP declining: cyclical pressures consistent with peak pessimism. US housing undersupply underpins demand; as #2 builder LEN captures a disproportionate volume-×-margin rebound when rates ease. We buy normalized earnings power.

old: Valuation is anchored to a normalized mid-cycle EPS (recovered volume × normalized margin), not to the depressed current level, applying a mid-cycle homebuilder multiple of ~10x. The return is generated by the E, not by multiple expansion — the current multiple would compress toward 10x, so the entire lift must come from the earnings recovery. The normalized margin is set below the pre-spin level (~10–11%, not the historical ~13%) to embed the permanent land-cost penalty: the asset-light model raised the cost of capital on land from roughly WACC (~7%) to the ~10% charged by land banks, some ~300bps of permanent margin drag. No ACOR add-back is applied, because at mid-cycle the deferral distortion has already self-cancelled — fees paid approximate fees recognized in COGS once the pipeline stops growing.
new: Valuation applies a ~10x mid-cycle multiple to normalized EPS (recovered volume × normalized margin); the multiple compresses, so all lift comes from earnings. Normalized margin (~10–11%, not historical ~13%) embeds ~300bps of permanent land-bank cost penalty. No ACOR add-back: at mid-cycle the deferral self-cancels.

old: LEN is a capital-return machine, with high payout ratios and a history of aggressive buybacks against a modest equity base. ACOR (accumulated option costs on real estate) is the stream of fees LEN pays to keep its land options alive: the fees accumulate on the balance sheet rather than hitting expense immediately, and only convert to cost when the home is delivered and sold. Once that fee drain reaches equilibrium (~FY27–28) and ACOR stops building, free cash flow would inflect positive and fund buybacks that are accretive at depressed prices.
new: LEN is a capital-return machine with high payouts and aggressive buybacks. ACOR, land-option fees accumulating on the balance sheet until homes are delivered, drains cash; once it reaches equilibrium (~FY27–28), FCF should inflect positive and fund buybacks accretive at depressed prices.

old: The trough keeps deepening with no visible inflection. If unit orders begin falling yoy for several consecutive Qs, the volume support breaks and the setup shifts from a cyclical trough to structural demand erosion driven by affordability.
new: The trough keeps deepening: if unit orders fall yoy for several consecutive Qs, volume support breaks and the cyclical trough becomes structural, affordability-driven demand erosion.

old: "Normal" proves worse than assumed, if incentives are structural rather than cyclical, if the land-cost penalty exceeds ~300bps, or if mid-cycle volume never returns to prior levels because affordability has permanently eroded.
new: "Normal" proves worse: incentives are structural, the land-cost penalty exceeds ~300bps, or mid-cycle volume never returns because affordability has permanently eroded.

old: The engine currently runs in reverse, with cash falling, net debt rising, and payouts funded from the balance sheet rather than from FCF. The thesis fails if ACOR equilibrium takes longer than FY27–28, or the cycle forces abandonment of land options, an irreversible cash loss, unlike the reversible non-cash impairments of the land-ownership previous model.
new: Payouts come from the balance sheet, not FCF. Fails if ACOR equilibrium slips past FY27–28 or the cycle forces abandoning land options: irreversible cash loss.

old: What is being bought is a 113-year-old ultra-luxury brand at trough volumes, with most of the value owed to creditors. At 34.56p (£0.3456; the LSE quote is in pence) and 1,009.6M shares, the market cap is £349M, sitting on £1,545M of net debt at H1 2026 (company definition, including £90M of leases and £39M of inventory financing). EV is about £1.89bn: 10.9x LTM adjusted EBITDA of £174M and 1.3x LTM revenue of £1,432M. The product range has been renewed (Vantage, DB12, Vanquish and DBX, now with S derivatives), and the Valhalla supercar is delivering: about 225 units in H1 2026 and around 500 guided for FY2026. Core volumes are still weak. Core wholesales were 5,266 in FY2025 against 5,812 in FY2024, and core ASP fell 5% in H1 2026 to £182k because of dealer support to clear aged stock.
new: A 113-year-old ultra-luxury brand at trough volumes, with most value owed to creditors: £349M market cap on £1,545M net debt (H1 2026), EV about £1.89bn, 10.9x LTM adjusted EBITDA. The range is renewed and Valhalla delivering, but core volumes remain weak.

old: The valuation uses EV/EBITDA on normalized FY2029E volumes rather than on Valhalla-inflated FY2026 figures, because Valhalla is a limited run that ends. Base: 5,700 core units at £205k, 220 Specials at about £1.0M wholesale ASP, and £150M of parts and other revenue give £1.54bn of revenue. At a 38.5% gross margin and £280M of cash opex, adjusted EBITDA is £312M (20%, against 18.7% in FY2023, the best year on record). At 8.0x, which is where AML traded on adjusted EBITDA in FY2022 to FY2024 and close to Porsche AG today, EV is £2.5bn. The equity is a thin residual. Capex of about £330M a year (a £1.7bn programme for FY2026 to FY2030) plus about £180M of cash interest exceeds EBITDA, so net debt keeps rising unless volumes and margin recover. Each turn of the multiple is worth about £310M, roughly the whole current market cap.
new: EV/EBITDA on normalized FY2029E, not Valhalla-inflated FY2026: £1.54bn revenue and £312M adjusted EBITDA at 8.0x give £2.5bn EV. Equity is a thin residual: capex (about £330M) plus interest (about £180M) exceeds EBITDA; each multiple turn is worth about £310M.

old: The return does not come from free cash flow, which was -£410M in FY2025 and -£198M in H1 2026. It depends on three things happening in order. First, EBITDA has to close the gap to capex plus interest, about £500M a year. Second, the $1,050M 10.0% and £565M 10.375% senior secured notes due March 2029 have to be refinanced without a debt-for-equity swap. Third, the strategic shareholders have to keep funding the gap: Lawrence Stroll's Yew Tree Consortium (32.99%), Geely (14.08%), PIF (13.88%) and Mercedes-Benz (7.54%), 68.5% combined at FY2025. Their record is to fund it, but at the cost of dilution (shares up about 23% since late 2023) and with related-party transactions attached. The July 2026 £450M HPS term loan was secured on trademarks moved into a new unrestricted subsidiary, and bondholders are threatening to challenge it. The position works as a call option. The base case is worth less than the current price, the bull case is worth about 6x, and the bear case leaves nothing for equity.
new: FCF is negative (-£410M FY2025): the return needs EBITDA to close the about £500M gap to capex plus interest, the March 2029 notes refinanced without debt-for-equity, and strategic shareholders (68.5%) to keep funding. A call option: base below price, bull about 6x, bear zero.
